Does not apply to open-ended health questions where a broad answer is acceptable.

payload.name: Enumerate-Affected-Group-Members-Before-Answering
payload.description: When a question asks 'who' was injured or affected within a named person's family or group, expand retrieval to role-based and relationship queries and verify evidence for every enumerated person before answering.
content: If the question asks 'who' was injured/affected in a named person's family or group, treat it as an enumeration question: search not only for the named person but also for each plausible family/group role (son, daughter, partner, etc.) using phrasing like '<named person>'s <role> injured'.

Before answering, check that every affected person you plan to name has direct evidence; a memory where the affected person is a relative and the named person is only the caretaker still counts as evidence for that relative.

Stop after the role-expanded searches return no new candidate or after you already have evidence identifying all affected individuals; do not exhaustively search every possible role when the current evidence is sufficient.

candidates.solves: The failure mechanism is that for 'who' questions about a named person's family or group, retrieval anchors on the named person alone and misses memories where the affected person is a relative or group member, producing incomplete answers. This applies to future questions of the form 'Who was injured/affected in [person]'s family/group?' where multiple individuals may be mentioned in separate memories. It does not apply to single-subject questions such as 'Was [person] injured?' or when the first evidence already enumerates all affected individuals.

payload.name: Per-entity retrieval for multi-subject questions
payload.description: Use before answering when a question asks what two or more named individuals experienced, encountered, or went through; run a targeted search per named individual and include event/incident-specific query variants.
content: When a question names multiple individuals and asks what each experienced or what incidents/events each had, run at least one targeted memory search per named individual, combining each individual's name with the event category from the question.

Add query expansions and keywords using discrete-event vocabulary (e.g., incident, episode, scare, emergency, wake-up call, hospitalization) alongside the question's wording, because specific events are often stored with different phrasing than the question.

Before answering, verify each named individual is supported by at least one retrieved memory; if any named individual has no supporting memory after the combined searches, run one additional targeted search for that individual. Stop once every named individual has a supporting memory or a targeted per-individual search with varied phrasings returns no new relevant results.

candidates.solves: Multi-entity questions can be answered after a joint search retrieves memories for only some named people, missing events stored with different vocabulary (e.g., 'incident', 'wake-up call'). Applies when a question names ≥2 individuals and asks what each experienced; run one targeted search per named individual with incident-specific variants and verify each is covered before answering. Does not apply to single-subject questions or when the initial search already supports every named individual.

payload.name: Expand stress-reliever queries with purpose synonyms
payload.description: When a question asks about a person's stress relievers or what helps them de-stress, include query expansions and keywords with synonyms like 'de-stress', 'relax', 'unwind', 'calm', 'soothe', and 'cope'.
content: When the question asks about a person's stress relievers or what helps them de-stress, include query expansions and keywords with synonyms such as 'de-stress', 'relax', 'unwind', 'calm', 'soothe', and 'cope'.
Also search for activities, places, or plans that mention these purposes (e.g., a plan to visit a scenic spot to de-stress) even if they do not use the phrase 'stress reliever'.
Stop after retrieving evidence for each claimed reliever or after a second diversified search; do not exhaustively expand.

candidates.solves: When a question asks about a person's stress relievers, a literal search for 'stress reliever' can miss memories that describe de-stressing activities or plans using words like 'de-stress' or 'relax'. This skill applies to future questions asking what relieves someone's stress or helps them unwind. It does not apply to generic preference or hobby questions that do not mention stress relief.

payload.name: Stress-source search fallback
payload.description: Use when a question asks about a person's main stressor or source of stress and initial retrieval returns only indirect or adjacent memories; conduct a targeted follow-up search using stress synonyms and any mentioned life domain before answering.
content: When a question asks about someone's main stressor or source of stress, do not answer from indirect memories alone (e.g., work-life balance, hobby limitations).
Run one additional hybrid or keyword search pairing the person's name with stress synonyms: stress, stressful, tough, pressure, overwhelmed, burnout.
If the first-pass results mention a specific domain (work, school, family, relationship), include that domain in the follow-up search (e.g., '<name> work stress').
Stop after one follow-up search if any returned memory explicitly states that a domain is stressful; otherwise continue with normal sufficiency checking.

candidates.solves: General failure: retrieval for stressor questions misses explicit memories that name a stressful domain (e.g., 'work has been tough and stressful') because initial queries use the noun 'stressor' and no stress synonyms. Applies when a future question asks about someone's main stressor or source of stress (with or without an exclusion like 'besides X') and the top results are only indirect (work-life balance, hobby limits). Does not apply when the first search already returns an explicit stressful-domain memory, or for non-stress questions.

payload.name: Venue-List Search Expansion
payload.description: When a question asks for the places/venues where a person submitted, entered, or published work (e.g., 'what places has X submitted to?'), use complementary venue-term searches before answering.
content: When the question is enumerative about submission/entry venues, do not answer from the first generic search alone.

After the initial search, run targeted searches for each obvious venue category in the domain (e.g., contest, competition, festival, exhibition, publication, conference) combined with the subject and a submission verb, and merge the evidence.

Stop after two consecutive venue-category searches yield no new submission/participation memories, or once the standard venue categories for that domain have been checked; do not search unrelated topics.

candidates.solves: The general failure is that an enumerative question about places/venues (e.g., 'what places has X submitted her work to?') is answered from a single generic search, so memories that name a different venue type (like a contest) are missed. This skill applies when the question asks for multiple submission/entry venues and the initial retrieval returns only one venue category or is sparse. It does not apply to single-venue questions, to non-venue questions, or when the first search already surfaces all relevant venue types.

payload.name: Travel destination retrieval with synonym coverage
payload.description: When a question asks where a person traveled/visited/went in a specific month or year and the first search returns no location memory, use travel-verb synonyms and a time-filtered event query before answering.
content: For questions asking where someone traveled, visited, or went in a specific month/year, if the initial hybrid search returns no memory containing a place, run one additional search that adds travel-verb synonyms such as 'road trip', 'trip', 'visit', 'traveled to', and 'went to' together with the time frame from the question.

Also issue a structured search over memory_kind='event' with world_start falling within the month/year named in the question; destination memories are often stored as events with a world_start date even when the text omits the word 'travel'.
Stop after this one extra retrieval pass; if still no memory with a destination appears, answer with the best available evidence or state that no information is available.

candidates.solves: When a question asks where a person traveled or visited in a specific month, the first hybrid search may miss the destination memory because the memory uses wording like 'road trip' rather than 'travel'. The Skill applies to future travel/location questions with a time window, requiring one extra search with travel-verb synonyms and an event/date-filtered structured query before concluding no information. It does not apply when initial results already contain a location or when the question is not about travels/destinations.

payload.name: Follow-up search for indirect state evidence
payload.description: When a question asks for the US state a named person was in during a stated activity/period and the first memory search returns no explicit location, run one additional search for the person's activities and named places, and treat a recognizable landmark's state as evidence.
content: If the question asks which US state a person was in during a stated activity/period (e.g., an internship) and the first search returns no explicit state, issue a follow-up search with the person's name plus location/activity clues such as 'visited', 'went to', 'at', 'in', 'hikes', 'trip', or any topic surfaced in the first results (e.g., a hobby or challenge).

If a returned memory names a recognizable US landmark (mountain, park, city, monument), map it to its state and use that as candidate evidence even if the memory says neither 'state' nor 'visited'. Stop after one such inference, or if the follow-up returns no named place and evidence sufficiency remains negative.

candidates.solves: Direct location searches can miss evidence when the only supporting memory records an activity at a recognizable place but omits the word 'state' and the region name. Applies when a question asks which US state a person visited during a stated period/internship and the first search returns only general context; then run one follow-up search for activity/location memories and, if a named landmark appears, infer its state as evidence. Does not apply when the memory explicitly names the state or when the question is not about a location.

payload.name: Count visits from place-anchored events
payload.description: When a question asks how many times a person has been to a specific city or country, and the memory evidence may describe actions that occurred there without using the word 'visit' or 'trip'.
content: Before answering a how-many-visits question, run a search that uses the place name itself (city and country) combined with the person's name, in addition to any literal 'visited <place>' query.

Count as a visit any distinct memory in which the person was present in that place, including receiving/giving something there, buying something there, attending an event there, or staying there; use the event date or world_start to separate distinct visits.
Stop expanding once the place-name search returns no new location-anchored events; do not enumerate every possible location synonym.

candidates.solves: Counting visits to a place fails when the only evidence is event memories that mention the place as the location of an action (e.g., received a gift, bought an item) rather than as a stated trip. The Skill applies to 'how many times has <person> been to <place>' questions where such place-anchored events exist; it must not be used when explicit visit/trip memories already answer the count, since the base retrieval is then sufficient.

payload.name: Location search via planned landmarks
payload.description: When a question asks for a person's location, US state, or whereabouts during a time period and direct searches do not surface an explicit location, apply this before concluding no information exists.
content: Before answering 'no information', search memory for the person's event/plan memories with world_start inside the target time window, using the person's name with activity or destination keywords found in their existing plans (e.g., visit, lake, trip, kayak).
If any retrieved plan/event names a geographic landmark, use that landmark as a query term in a follow-up search; when the landmark is tied to a state, use that to answer the location question.

Stop after one confirming follow-up if the landmark resolves the location; if the landmark spans multiple states, report those states or use other retrieved context to disambiguate, and do not enumerate landmarks beyond those already present in the retrieved memories.

candidates.solves: Generic location queries miss plan/event memories whose named landmarks imply the state. Applies to future 'Which US state was X in during [month/year]?' questions where an event/plan in that window names a place. Exclude cases where direct search already reveals an explicit location, or where no landmark-bearing plan/event exists in the window.

payload.name: Per-person travel overlap retrieval
payload.description: When a question asks which city/place several named people both visited and initial combined search lacks travel memories for one, search per person with travel synonyms (visited, went, trip, been to) and any candidate city names before concluding no evidence.
content: Before answering a multi-person shared-place question, if the combined search did not return travel/location memories for every named person, run one bounded search per person using their name plus travel synonyms (visited, went, took a trip, traveled, been to).
When a retrieved memory names a candidate place, include that place name in a follow-up search for the other person(s), and account for close name variants (e.g., Jon/John) when matching.

Stop once each person has relevant travel memories or after one search per person plus one candidate-place follow-up; then intersect the places. Do not repeat identical combined queries, and do not exhaustively enumerate all possible places.

candidates.solves: Multi-person shared-place questions fail when one literal combined query misses memories phrased with travel synonyms or explicit place names and the agent concludes 'no information.' Applies when asking which city/place two or more named people both visited and initial retrieval lacks evidence for one person; not when the combined search already supplies sufficient travel memories or the question is single-person.

payload.name: Destination-name retrieval for country-travel questions
payload.description: Use when the user asks which countries or places someone has traveled to or visited, and the first retrieval does not return an explicit country list.
content: When answering 'which countries/places did [person] travel to or visit?', run a keyword search using the person's name plus at least the verb variants 'visited', 'traveled', 'went to', and 'trip' (memory_kinds ['event'], depth 'deep', top_k >= 8) before concluding no travel memories exist.

Examine retrieved event memories for named cities, regions, or countries. If a memory names only a city or region, add that destination name to one follow-up search (e.g., '[person] [destination]') and inspect the result for additional country-level travel evidence.

Stop after two consecutive searches return no new destination mentions; then answer using the countries either stated in, or unambiguously implied by, the retrieved destination evidence. Do not answer from a single vacation memory when the question asks for a list.

candidates.solves: Generic travel-history searches can miss memories that name a specific city or region instead of a country, causing the agent to answer prematurely from a single trip mention. This Skill applies to future 'which countries/places did [person] travel to or visit' questions when initial retrieval returns only broad trip or activity memories. It should not be used when the question already names a specific country or when retrieval already contains the full list of destination countries.

payload.name: Expand retrieval for all visited locations
payload.description: When answering a question that asks for all places a person has visited or been to, and the first search returns only general travel stories, use this Skill to broaden the query and verify coverage before answering.
content: If the question asks for all visited locations (e.g., 'Where has X been?', 'What locations has X visited?'), run an additional search using the person's name together with location-oriented phrases such as 'went to', 'visited', 'trip', 'traveled to', and 'took a photo in'.

Do not stop at the first result set. Inspect retrieved memories that describe any geographic setting even if the exact place name is not in the original query, and check whether each such location is already in your evidence list.

Before finalizing an enumerative answer, explicitly verify that every location you found across the retrieved memories is covered by the evidence version IDs you cite; if a location appears only in a memory you did not inspect, inspect it and add it when supported.

candidates.solves: When a question asks to enumerate all geographical locations a person has visited, a single hybrid top-k search often misses memories where the location is embedded inside a broader event narrative, leading to incomplete answers. This Skill applies when answering such list-style location questions and guides expanding retrieval with location-oriented terms and verifying coverage before answering. It should not apply to questions about a single specific location or to non-location enumeration questions.

payload.name: InferRegionFromCityLocation
payload.description: When a question asks which state, province, or country a person visited and the initial memory search returns no location, search again for city-level location memories about the person and infer the region from the city before answering.
content: If a question asks for an administrative region (state, province, country) a person visited and the first search returns no usable location memory, run one additional search using city-level terms (city, town, beach, went to) combined with the person's name.
When the additional search returns a city, use standard geographic knowledge to infer the region (e.g., Tampa → Florida) and answer with the inferred region, citing the city memory as evidence.
Do not continue searching further if no city or region is found; answer 'No information available' and stop.

candidates.solves: Retrieval fails because the answer is stored at city level (e.g., Tampa) while the question asks for a region (e.g., Florida), and the agent stops after one empty search. Use when a question asks which state, province, or country a person visited and direct search finds no region; search city-level locations and infer the region from the city. Do not use when the region is already present in retrieved memory or the question is not about a geographic region.

payload.name: Location-mention recall via event/plan search
payload.description: When a question asks which cities/places a person mentioned, visited, or plans to explore and the first retrieval returns only past-travel results, run an additional event/plan-focused search with location and travel-expansion terms before answering.
content: When a question asks which cities, countries, or places a person mentioned, visited, or plans to explore, do not restrict queries to the verb 'visit' or past-tense travel language; include travel-intent expansions such as 'explore', 'trip', 'game/match at', 'favorite city', and 'plan to go'.

If the first pass returns no location-bearing memories for that person or misses expected locations, run one additional structured or hybrid search combining the person's name with location tokens (city/country names, 'city', 'travel', 'trip', 'event') and accept event/plan memories that name a location even without the word 'visit'.
Stop once the distinct locations recoverable from the person's event/plan/travel memories have been enumerated; do not perform per-city exhaustive searches.

candidates.solves: Retrieval for questions asking which places a person mentioned can miss memories that express locations via future events, plans, or preferences rather than the literal verb 'visit'. Future 'which cities did X mention' questions should trigger an additional event/plan-focused search with location and travel-expansion terms. Not for stated-opinion or simple past-travel questions where standard keyword search already suffices.

payload.name: Search preference and state kinds for activity questions
payload.description: Use when a question asks what someone read, watched, or engaged in during a time period and the first search restricted to event memories returns no direct evidence; re-run including preference and state kinds.
content: Before answering an activity question (e.g., what book someone read, what show someone watched), if the initial search was limited to memory_kind 'event' and lacks direct evidence, issue an additional hybrid search without memory_kind restriction or including 'preference' and 'state'.
Ongoing activities such as 'currently reading X' are often stored as preference memories; do not discard them just because the memory kind is not event.
Stop after this broader search returns a version with the subject's activity; do not exhaustively expand queries.

candidates.solves: The general failure is over-restricting memory_kind to 'event' in activity questions, causing preference/state memories about ongoing reading or media use to be missed and leading to a wrong answer. Applies when a future question asks what a person read, watched, or otherwise engaged in over a period and the first event-only search shows no direct evidence. Does not apply to questions about discrete one-time events where event memories are the correct target and no preference/state memory describes the activity.

payload.name: Origin search for introduction questions
payload.description: When a question asks how a person was introduced to or first started an ongoing activity, and the initial retrieval returns no childhood, family, or origin memory, run one targeted origin search before answering.
content: When the question asks about the origin of an ongoing activity (e.g., how someone got introduced to basketball), first check whether the retrieved memories include any early-life, family, or starting-point context.

If no such memory is present, issue exactly one additional search adding origin terms (childhood, started, family, father) to the activity, and inspect compound memories where the activity is a secondary detail.
Stop after that search and answer only from visible evidence; do not perform exhaustive expansions.

candidates.solves: Origin-question failures where initial retrieval returns only recent activity memories and misses an early-life/family memory describing the activity's start. Applies when a future question asks how someone was introduced to or first started an ongoing activity and initial results lack any origin/family/childhood context. Does not apply when initial results already contain an explicit origin memory, or for non-origin questions about current activities or events.

payload.name: Search plan and event memories for scheduled activities
payload.description: When a user asks when someone is attending, visiting, or participating in a future or scheduled activity (e.g., conference, appointment, trip), include plan memories in the search before concluding no information is available.
content: When the question asks about a future or scheduled activity (attending, visiting, participating), do not restrict memory_kinds to event; include plan memories in the hybrid or structured search.

If the first search returns no direct match, retry with a broader memory_kind filter (include plan, and profile if relevant) and query terms like 'plans to attend', 'will attend', or 'next month' before answering 'No information available'.
Stop once a relevant plan or event memory is found; do not exhaustively search all kinds when sufficient evidence is retrieved.

candidates.solves: When a user asks about a future or scheduled activity (e.g., 'When is Tim attending a book conference?'), the agent may restrict the search to event-kind memories and miss the plan memory that contains the date. This Skill applies to any future or scheduled activity query where the answer may be stored as a plan; before answering 'no information', search both plan and event memory kinds (or without kind restriction) and resolve relative-time phrases. It does not apply to questions about past events or preferences where event-only search is already sufficient.

payload.name: Search repeated-behavior memories for emerging-theme questions
payload.description: When a question asks about an emerging/recurring theme, pattern, or what someone is becoming known for in their life, use behavior-focused query variants and a structured subject search instead of resubmitting the same literal query.
content: If the question asks what theme or pattern is emerging in a person's life, or what they are becoming known for, do not search only the abstract phrase; build query variants from concrete repeated behaviors and interactions (e.g., helping, encountering, volunteering, recurring activities).
Run a hybrid search with those behavior-focused variants and also run one structured search filtered to that person as subject to retrieve their event and interaction memories.
Stop after at most two distinct search formulations; then judge whether any returned memory describes a recurring behavior or repeated interaction, and answer only from visible evidence.

candidates.solves: Access searches for questions about a person's emerging or recurring life theme often fail because the agent resubmits the same abstract query and never searches for the person's concrete repeated behaviors or interactions. This skill applies when a question asks what theme/pattern is emerging in someone's life or what they are becoming known for, as described by another person. It does not apply to direct fact questions that already contain the concrete activity keyword.

payload.name: IncludeEventKindForCurrentActivitySearches
payload.description: When a question asks about a person's current ongoing activity (reading, watching, working on), search event memories as well as state memories before concluding no information.
content: When the question asks what someone is currently reading, watching, working on, or otherwise doing as an ongoing activity, include memory_kind 'event' in the search; do not restrict to 'state' only.
If the first search returns no evidence matching the activity, retry with memory_kinds extended to include 'event' (and 'state' if excluded) before answering 'No information available'.
Stop as soon as a memory directly naming the activity and the subject is found; do not exhaustively search all memory kinds when evidence is sufficient.

candidates.solves: General failure: retrieval is restricted to state memories for questions about ongoing activities, causing event-stored activities to be missed. Applies when a user asks what someone is currently reading, watching, working on, or otherwise doing; include the event memory kind in the search. Does not apply to questions about stable attributes or preferences, and does not mandate exhaustive search when evidence is already sufficient.

payload.name: Find competing interests for delayed activities
payload.description: When a question asks why a person delayed, put off, or avoided a recurring activity and the initial memory search only returns memories about that activity, before answering, search for the person's alternative interests, hobbies, and preferred activities.
content: When a question asks why someone put off, delayed, skipped, or avoided a recurring activity (e.g., yoga, exercise, study), and the first retrieval only found memories about that activity, run an additional semantic search combining the person's name with terms like 'enjoys', 'prefers', 'loves', 'interest', 'hobby', or 'passion'.

When comparing evidence for procrastination or avoidance, treat a strong competing interest as a candidate explanation; do not default to the only reasons found within the delayed activity's own memories.
Stop after one or two additional searches and answer only from retrieved, visible evidence; do not infer unstated preferences.

candidates.solves: Retrieval misses competing interests when a 'why did X delay Y' question is answered only from Y-related memories while the true cause is an alternative hobby. Applies to any future question asking why someone put off, delayed, skipped, or avoided a recurring activity when initial searches return only activity-specific memories. Must not apply when the delay is already explained by external events, scheduling, or explicit statements in retrieved evidence.

payload.name: Broaden Plan Queries Beyond Plan Memory Kind
payload.description: When a question asks about a person's future projects/plans and a search filtered to 'plan' memories returns no strong evidence, re-search with broader memory kinds and interest-based phrasing.
content: When a question asks about a person's plans or projects, do not rely solely on memory_kinds=['plan']; include kinds such as 'event', 'preference', and 'state' in the search.

If the first search yields no strong evidence, run one follow-up search using the person's name with interest/focus verbs (e.g., 'interested in', 'focused on', 'working on') and avoid a narrow time window derived solely from 'next year' unless a specific date is stated.
Stop after the follow-up search and answer from the best available evidence; do not expand to unrelated searches.

candidates.solves: Future-oriented questions about a person's projects can miss memories stored as interests or ongoing focuses under kinds like 'event' or 'preference' when the agent over-restricts to 'plan' memories. Apply when the user asks what someone is planning/doing next and the initial kind-filtered search is weak. Do not apply when a normal plan-kind search already returns directly relevant, high-confidence memories.

payload.name: Appearance-change retrieval for abstract transformation queries
payload.description: When a question asks about a person's physical transformation, appearance change, or looks within a time period, retrieve concrete appearance-change event memories instead of relying on abstract query terms.
content: When the question asks about a person's physical transformation or appearance change in a time window, expand the query with concrete appearance-change phrases (dyed, cut, shaved, tattoo, pierced, glasses, gained/lost weight) and add structured or keyword searches on event memories with those terms.
If the first round returns only unrelated topical memories and no appearance-related event, run at least one more search targeting appearance terms before answering 'no information'.

candidates.solves: The failure occurs when abstract appearance wording like 'physical transformation' misses concrete appearance-change events (e.g., dyed hair) in memory search. The Skill applies when a future question asks what physical or appearance change a person underwent in a stated time window, and instructs the agent to search with concrete appearance-change terms and inspect event memories near the target date. It does not apply to ordinary event-retrieval questions that do not describe appearance changes.

payload.name: EnumerationHowQuestionsFollowUp
payload.description: When a user asks how a person achieved, promoted, created, or improved something (an enumeration 'how' question) and the initial memory search returns mostly general statements about the person/entity, run additional targeted searches for that person's specific actions or events before answering.
content: Detect enumeration-type 'how' questions ('How did X promote/start/improve/create...?') that ask for concrete steps or methods; do not treat general state or status memories as a complete answer.

After the first retrieval, if the question implies multiple methods and the evidence contains few distinct event/action memories about the subject, run at least one follow-up search: pair the subject with action-oriented terms (made, created, developed, launched, partnered) or use a structured search of event memories filtered by subject and sorted by recency; merge results before the sufficiency check.
Stop after one or two follow-ups when no new distinct actions appear or each relevant time period has at least one concrete method; do not exhaustively list all memories.

candidates.solves: For 'how did X do Y' questions, the agent may answer from top-k general memories and miss specific action/event memories that lack the question's keywords. This skill applies when a future question asks for a person's methods or steps (e.g., promote, create, improve, start a business) and the first search returns mostly state summaries; it instructs the agent to run follow-up targeted/structured searches for the subject's concrete events before judging sufficiency. It must not apply to questions answered by a single fact or descriptor where the initial retrieval already suffices.

payload.name: Activity-during-condition hobby search
payload.description: When a question asks what activity a person does while recovering from or coping with a condition, and initial results only show treatment/exercise memories, search for that person's hobbies or pastimes before answering.
content: If the question asks for an activity someone does during a period (e.g., while healing) and no memory explicitly links an activity to that period, run an additional search using the person's name plus hobby-related terms such as 'hobby', 'enjoy', 'relax', or 'pastime'.
Treat retrieved hobby/interest memories as candidate answers if they are temporally plausible relative to the period.
Stop after one supplementary hobby search unless it returns no hobby memories; do not expand to unrelated topics.

candidates.solves: Answers about what activity a person does during a recovery or similar period fail when only condition-focused memories are retrieved and the correct evidence is a hobby memory not explicitly linked to the condition. This Skill applies to future questions phrasing an activity during a condition/period and a first search returning only treatment/recovery memories. It must not apply when the question already names an activity type or the retrieved memory directly states the activity.

payload.name: Infer Age From Life-Stage Evidence
payload.description: When asked for a person's age and no direct age or birthdate memory is found, search for life-stage indicators (student, school, classes, internship, finals) before concluding no information.
content: When a question asks for a person's age and no memory directly states age or birthdate, do not answer 'no information' after the first search. Run one additional search for that person using life-stage terms such as 'student', 'school', 'classes', 'internship', or 'finals'.

If that search or already-returned memories show the person is currently a student (e.g., taking classes, studying for finals, or interning), answer with a hedged inference such as 'likely a current student, so probably in the typical student age range', cite the supporting memories, and mark the answer as an inference with moderate confidence.
Stop after the one additional search; do not broaden to unrelated topics. If no direct or life-stage evidence is found, answer 'no information available'.

candidates.solves: The general failure is answering 'no information' for an age question after a single literal keyword search, ignoring indirect evidence such as student status. This Skill applies when a future question asks for a person's age and no explicit age memory exists, but memories about school, studies, classes, or internships can support a likely age range. It does not apply when a direct age or birthdate memory exists, and it does not apply to non-age attributes that cannot be inferred from life stage.

payload.name: Indirect meeting search for role questions
payload.description: Apply when a question asks when or how a person met a role-identified person (future wife, spouse) and direct role-based queries return no evidence; search the person's name with meeting/trip terms and inspect event memories.
content: Before answering 'no information', if the question asks when or how a person met a role-identified person (future wife, spouse, partner), retry retrieval with the person's name plus broad terms: met, met someone, trip, vacation, encounter, woman.

Treat an event memory about a meeting or trip (e.g., 'met an amazing Canadian woman on a trip') as relevant evidence even if it omits the role label; use its world_start or the message timestamp to answer when.
Stop after two or three such targeted searches if no meeting event appears; do not exhaustively expand.

candidates.solves: The failure mechanism is that relational labels (future wife, spouse) in the question do not match event memories that describe the meeting indirectly (e.g., 'met an amazing woman on a trip'). Future pattern: 'when did X meet his/her wife/partner' with no explicit role in stored events. Applies when the event lacks the role label; not when the event explicitly states the role or the question already contains the date.

payload.name: Broaden retrieval for off-skill career goals
payload.description: When a question asks about a person's career goals explicitly excluding their primary professional skill or domain (e.g., 'not related to his main skill', 'aspirations outside his field'), use this to broaden retrieval.
content: When a question asks about goals or aspirations explicitly outside a person's primary skill or domain (e.g., 'not related to', 'outside', 'beyond' that skill), do not restrict memory_kinds to profile/state; include preference, event, and plan, because off-skill ambitions like endorsements, charity, and business ventures are stored there.

Add query variations that name concrete off-skill goal categories such as endorsements, brand building, charity, community work, or side ventures, and run at least one search for those terms instead of only rewording the question.
Stop as soon as retrieved memories cover the distinct goal categories mentioned in the question, or after two searches with the broader kinds/terms; do not list every possible goal.

candidates.solves: Retrieval misses goals stored outside profile/state when a question contrasts a person's main skill with other career goals, because the agent restricts memory kinds and only paraphrases the question. Applies to future questions phrased as 'goals not related to X' or 'aspirations outside X' for any person/domain. Does not apply when the question concerns the main skill itself or when the goals are already captured in profile/state.

payload.name: Trait_Search_For_Future_Options
payload.description: When a question asks what a person could do, possible career paths, or future actions, and the retrieved plan/future memories only partially support an answer, search again using the person's values, interests, and demonstrated helping/teaching/leadership behaviors before concluding.
content: Before answering a 'what could X do' / 'future career or path' question, if the first retrieval returns only explicit plans or current activities, run one additional search that includes terms for the person's known traits and enacted behaviors (e.g., helping, mentoring, sharing knowledge, leadership, giving back), not just the explicit topic.
Do not expand this to exhaustive search: after this one additional trait-based search, if no new supporting evidence appears, proceed with the evidence already retrieved.

candidates.solves: When a question asks what a person could do in the future, topic-focused retrieval misses semantically distant memories about the person's values and demonstrated behaviors (e.g., teaching, helping, leadership) that would support an informed answer. Apply this skill to future-option questions where the initial search returns only explicit plans or current activities; run one additional search using trait and behavior terms. Do not apply to factual recall questions or when the initial retrieval already provides sufficient evidence.

payload.name: Per-Person Search for Shared Experiences
payload.description: When a question asks about a shared frustration, problem, preference, or experience between two named people, search each person's memories individually with topic and negative/desire terms before concluding no information.
content: If the question asks for a common/shared frustration, problem, preference, or experience between two named people, do not search only once with both names and the attribute in one query.
Run separate searches for each person alone using the topic and negative/desire predicates such as searching, looking for, not found, unable, difficulty, wants, or needs.

After retrieving per-person memories, check whether any pair describes the same topic or complementary frustration; only answer 'no information' after at least one such per-person search for each person with negative terms, then stop.

candidates.solves: The general failure is answering 'shared experience' questions with a single query that requires one memory to mention both names and the attribute, which misses separate per-person memories that jointly establish common ground. This applies to future questions asking about a frustration, problem, preference, or experience shared by two named people, where evidence may exist in individual memories of each person. It does not apply to questions about only one person or to factual questions where a single memory should contain the complete answer.

payload.name: Temporal decomposition for activity-spending questions
payload.description: When a question asks how a person spends time with a companion after a life event, during a trip, or in a period, search planned/upcoming and recently dated events separately and require evidence for multiple distinct activities before answering.
content: If the question asks how X spends time with Y after/around an event or during a period, run separate searches for planned or upcoming events (e.g., honeymoon, trips, gatherings) and for recently dated events with Y, using temporal filters such as month names or 'this weekend' when the context provides them.

After each search, check whether evidence covers distinct activities implied by the question; if only one tangential memory (e.g., an older trip) is retrieved, search again with activity synonyms (ski, snowshoe, cuisine, get-together, celebration) before answering.
Do not answer an open-ended 'how does X spend time' question from a single memory; collect at least two evidence pieces from different time windows, then stop once the activities are covered.

candidates.solves: Open-ended questions about how someone spends time with a companion after a life event are often answered from one semantically similar memory, missing planned future events and recent dated events. This Skill applies when a future question asks how a person spends or spent time with a named companion after an event, during a trip, or around a date, where the answer spans multiple events; it does not apply when the question targets one specific event or date where a single memory suffices.

payload.name: RecentRewardingExperienceAchievementSearch
payload.description: When a question asks about a person's recent rewarding, fulfilling, or positive experience and the initial search returns sentiment-matching events.
content: When a question asks about a person's recent rewarding, fulfilling, or positive experience, expand the search with achievement/recognition terms (e.g., presented, conference, award, positive feedback, recognized) in addition to the literal sentiment words; such experiences are often stored as achievement events.

When the question says 'recently', compare the world_start dates of retrieved candidates and prefer the most recent; if the top candidates are clearly older than other events in the results, re-run with a recency filter instead of answering from an old memory.
Answer only when a candidate matches both recency and the positive-outcome aspect; if only one dimension matches, search again before answering.

candidates.solves: Sentiment-focused searches for 'recent rewarding experience' miss achievement events (presentations, feedback, awards) and may settle on older matches. Applies when the question asks about a person's recent rewarding/fulfilling/positive experience and first retrieval returns multiple candidates: add achievement/recognition terms, use world_start dates to choose the most recent, and don't answer from an older candidate. Not for queries that already name the concrete activity.

payload.name: Multi-person recommendation shared-interest search
payload.description: When a question asks for a gift or other recommendation intended for two or more named people, and the initial retrieval lacks explicit shared-activity evidence.
content: When a question asks for a recommendation (e.g., a gift) for multiple named people, do not rely only on a generic query. Also search for shared interests or joint activities between those people, such as classes they both attend, recipes or meals they exchanged, common hobbies, or plans they made together.

If the first retrieval returns only general profile/state memories or evidence for one person, run one or two targeted searches combining each person's name with activity terms (e.g., cooking, class, hobby, shared, together) until you find a memory that links them.

Ground the final recommendation in that shared-interest memory if one is found; otherwise, use each person's individual preferences and note the compromise. Stop once the shared-interest search yields a concrete supporting memory, rather than exhaustively exploring every activity.

candidates.solves: The agent failed to retrieve shared-interest memories when answering a multi-person recommendation question: after one generic retrieval about gifts and healthy lifestyles, it answered without a follow-up for the shared cooking/recipe activity between Evan and Sam. Future questions like 'what gift would suit both X and Y?' benefit from an explicit search for joint activities or exchanged interests. It should not apply to single-person recommendation questions or when the initial retrieval already contains direct shared-activity evidence.

payload.name: Shared-event query disambiguation
payload.description: When a question asks what one person shared with another (achievement, news, event), treat 'shared' as possibly meaning one person told/mentioned the other about a personal event, and broaden point-time searches to a nearby range if the first search misses evidence.
content: When a question asks what one person shared with another (achievement, news, event), treat 'shared' as potentially meaning one person told/mentioned the other about a personal event, not only a joint activity. Add query expansions like 'X told Y about', 'X mentioned to Y', 'X reported to Y' and search for X's own events/achievements near the time.
If a point-time search returns no usable evidence, retry with a time range around the target (e.g., ±2 weeks) before answering 'No information available'; stop once sufficient evidence is found.

candidates.solves: When a question asks what one person shared with another (e.g., 'What achievement did X share with Y?'), the retriever may overspecify 'shared' as a joint/collaborative event and anchor time to a single point, thereby missing a personal achievement that one person disclosed to the other near the target date. This Skill applies to future relational questions where the answer may be one party's own recent event mentioned to the other. It must not apply when the question explicitly asks for a joint activity or when the first search already returns sufficient evidence.

payload.name: PerPersonWindowSearchForConversationTopics
payload.description: When a question asks what named people discussed or talked about on a specific date, search each person's memories for that date and a short preceding window, include event memories not phrased as 'discussion', and combine all topics found before answering.
content: When asked what named people discussed on a specific date D, first search memories for each named person with the date and a short preceding window (e.g., D-3 to D), not requiring the words 'discuss' or 'talk'.
Treat event memories whose world_start falls in that window as candidate discussion topics for that person, even if the memory only describes one person's activity on that day or shortly before.

Combine candidates from all named people; if they represent multiple distinct topics, report all topics. Stop after one per-person date-window search for each name, and answer only when no additional window-aligned events remain.

candidates.solves: The general failure is answering a 'what did they discuss on date D' question from the first single-memory hit, which misses another participant's date- or window-aligned event memory that is also a discussion topic, yielding a one-topic answer. Applies to future questions that ask what two or more named people talked about on an exact calendar date, including recent events they are likely to have revisited. Does not apply when a memory already explicitly describes the conversation topic and sufficiency checks confirm no other window-aligned events.

payload.name: Retrieve individual profiles for shared-interest questions
payload.description: When a question asks what interests, hobbies, or activities two named people share, search each person's profile/hobby memories separately and intersect before answering.
content: When a question asks what interests, hobbies, or activities two named people share, run a separate hybrid search for each person's profile (e.g., '<Name> hobbies' or '<Name> interests') in addition to any joint query.

Base the answer on the intersection of the two individuals' profile/preference memories; do not treat a plan or event of doing something together (e.g., hiking invitation, cooking session) as evidence of a shared interest unless the individual profiles confirm it.
Stop after retrieving each person's profile/hobby memories and the joint results; answer from the intersection, without exhaustive expansion.

candidates.solves: General failure mechanism: an agent answers questions about shared interests between two people using only retrieval of joint-activity event/plan memories, missing the individual profile memories that state the actual hobbies. Future pattern: any question of the form 'What interests/hobbies do X and Y share?' or 'What common interests do X and Y have?'. Non-applicable: questions about a single person's interests or about past joint activities/events, where profile intersection is not needed.

payload.name: Common-ground-between-two-people
payload.description: When the user asks what two named people have in common, how they are similar, or what they both share, retrieve and compare each person's individual event/state memories for parallel life facts instead of relying on relationship memories alone.
content: When the question asks what two named people have in common or how they are similar, do not rely only on relationship or support memories; run an additional targeted search for each person's individual event and state memories (career, employment, business, major changes) using filters or structured queries per person.

Compare the two individual profiles and require at least one matching fact type or event across both persons before answering; if the proposed commonality is a shared life change, cite one memory per person as evidence.
Stop after two targeted searches per person if no parallel individual facts emerge; do not exhaustively enumerate all memories.

candidates.solves: The failure is answering a two-person commonality question from relationship or support memories only, which misses parallel individual facts such as both losing a job or both starting businesses. The Skill applies to future questions that ask what two named people have in common or how they are similar, when the answer may lie in comparable personal events or states. It must not apply to single-person questions or to questions that only ask how the two people relate to each other.

payload.name: BroadenKindsForFuturePlansAndProjects
payload.description: When a question asks about a person's upcoming plans, projects, or goals, do not restrict memory_kind to 'plan' only; include event and state kinds or structured predicate search.
content: When a question asks about a person's future plans, projects, or goals (e.g., 'what is X planning for next year?', 'what projects does X have upcoming?'), do not limit the first search to memory_kind 'plan'. Plans and projects are often stored as 'event' or 'state' memories with predicates like 'project', 'plan', or 'goal'.

Run at least one retrieval that includes memory_kinds ['event', 'state', 'plan'] or omits the kind filter, or perform a structured search by predicate 'project'/'plan' with the same person and relevant time window, before concluding evidence is insufficient.
Stop as soon as sufficient supporting evidence is found; do not add extra topic-specific searches or expand the time window further.

candidates.solves: When a question asks about a person's upcoming plans, projects, or goals, the retrieval can over-narrow by filtering memory_kind to 'plan' based on the question's surface wording, causing relevant memories stored as 'event' or 'state' (e.g., predicate 'project') to be missed. This Skill applies to future questions like 'What is X planning/projecting for next year/period?' where the memory store may use multiple kinds for planning-related content. It does not apply when the schema guarantees all plans use kind 'plan' or when the question explicitly targets a stored plan object.

payload.name: Rephrase and Retry Before No-Answer
payload.description: Use when a search for a named fact, motto, phrase, or quote returns no memory that directly answers the question; before answering 'No information available,' retry with rephrased and semantically equivalent wording.
content: Before answering 'No information available' after a search, run at least one additional search with a rephrased query when the question asks for a specific named fact, motto, phrase, or attribute value. Include possessive forms, synonyms, and related descriptive terms (e.g., 'family's motto' in addition to 'family motto').

Prefer a hybrid or semantic search strategy for the rephrased query. Stop after one additional search unless the new results suggest a clearly promising additional variation; do not keep expanding queries indefinitely.
If the rephrased search also yields no relevant evidence, answer 'No information available' with the evidence explicitly listed.

candidates.solves: This addresses premature 'no information' answers when the only matching memory uses different wording than the query. It applies when a question asks for a specific named fact, motto, phrase, or attribute value and the initial keyword search misses a semantically equivalent memory. It does not apply when the first search already returns sufficient evidence, or when no plausible rephrasing exists.

payload.name: Follow-up location search for activity events
payload.description: When answering a 'where did [person] [discover/do] [thing]?' question and the most relevant memory names the activity but not its location.
content: Before answering a location question, inspect the evidence memory for an explicit location. If the directly relevant memory (e.g., discovering a dive spot) has no place, run one additional search combining the person, a time window around that memory's date, and location terms such as trip, traveled, visited, retreat, city, or country.

Prefer the memory that explicitly mentions the activity asked about; do not answer with a thematically similar memory (like a waterfall or beach) unless it also mentions that activity. Stop once a location-bearing memory from the same time window is found.

candidates.solves: When the best activity memory lacks its location, the agent answers from a thematically similar but unrelated memory instead of searching for a second memory that places the person at a place in the same time window. Applies to 'Where did [person] find/do [thing]?' when the activity memory omits location. Not for memories that already state a location or for general preference questions.

payload.name: PreciseObjectForMissingPreferenceAnswers
payload.description: When a question asks what a person misses, longs for, or finds lacking in a place, use the exact object named in a directly relevant retrieved memory rather than a broader synonym.
content: When a user asks what X misses/longs for/lacks in a location, first check whether any retrieved memory states the missed object explicitly (e.g., 'X misses nature').
If such an explicit statement exists, answer with that specific object (or a close paraphrase of it) instead of a broader category that the same evidence might also imply.
If no retrieved memory names the object explicitly, proceed with the usual synthesis from multiple memories; do not force an unstated object.

candidates.solves: When answering what someone misses, longs for, or finds lacking in a place, the model may answer with a broader synonym even though a retrieved memory directly states the exact missed object, causing a mismatch with the expected precise answer. This Skill applies to user questions explicitly asking what a person misses/wants/lacks in a setting, whenever a retrieved memory contains a direct statement of the missed object. It does not apply when no such direct statement exists and the answer must be synthesized from multiple indirect memories.

payload.name: BroadenMemoryKindsForVisitedPlaces
payload.description: When a question asks which cities or places a person has visited or been to, and a memory search restricts memory_kinds to a single kind, broaden or remove the filter before searching.
content: When a question asks to enumerate the cities or places a person has visited or been to, do not set memory_kinds to only 'event'. Include 'plan' and 'state' kinds, or omit the memory_kinds filter entirely, because travel history can be recorded under any memory kind.
Run at least one search with the broadened or removed filter and merge the results before forming the answer, so relevant memories of different kinds are not missed.
Stop once the evidence is sufficient to list the places; do not run further searches for every possible location.

candidates.solves: The general failure is that a memory_kind filter (e.g., only 'event') can exclude relevant travel-history memories stored under 'plan' or 'state', causing an incomplete answer when a question enumerates a person's visited cities. This Skill applies to future questions asking which cities or places a person has visited or been to, when the first search restricts memory_kinds to a single kind. It must not apply to questions about a person's opinions/recommendations of cities or purely future planned destinations, which are not evidence of past visits.

payload.name: Supplementary Activity Retrieval
payload.description: When a question asks what a person does to supplement, complement, or do in addition to a primary activity, use this before answering to retrieve all distinct supplementary activities rather than stopping after the first supporting memory.
content: When a question asks what a person does to supplement, complement, or add to a primary activity (e.g., 'to supplement his training'), do not stop after the first search returns one supporting memory; the question often expects a set of distinct supplementary activities.

Run at least one additional search with the primary activity name removed; use complementary-activity descriptors (e.g., flexibility, stretching, conditioning, recovery, cross-training) and generic terms like 'workout' or 'exercise routine', because the supplementary activity memory may not mention the primary activity.

Before answering, compare the distinct activities found across all retrieved memories; if only one distinct supplementary activity is found but the question implies multiple (e.g., 'and', 'supplement', plural intent), run one more broader search before concluding sufficiency.
Stop adding searches once an additional search returns no new distinct supplementary activity; do not exhaustively list every possible activity.

candidates.solves: Failure: 'supplement'/'in addition to' questions are answered after one search anchored on the primary activity, missing activities whose memories omit that term. Applies to future questions asking what a person does extra for a main activity; requires a second search without the main activity and checking for multiple distinct activities. Not for plain 'what does X do?' or when the first search already returns multiple distinct activities.

payload.name: Category-question concrete-instance search
payload.description: When a question asks for activities or items in a broad category (e.g., outdoor activities, hobbies, foods) and initial retrieval returns no concrete instances, run additional searches using common concrete examples of that category with the subject's name.
content: When a question asks for a list in a broad category (e.g., outdoor activities, hobbies, foods) and the initial search returns no memories naming concrete items, run 1-2 additional hybrid or keyword searches pairing the subject's name with common concrete examples of that category (e.g., for outdoor: surfing, hiking, running, cycling). Stop once relevant concrete-item memories are found; do not enumerate exhaustively.

candidates.solves: Category-label questions (e.g., 'What outdoor activities does John enjoy?') can fail when memories store concrete instances (e.g., surfing) without the category label, so a search using only the category phrase misses them. This Skill applies when a question asks for a list of items in a broad category and the first retrieval returns no concrete items; it instructs running additional searches using common concrete examples of that category with the subject's name. It does not apply when the initial search already surfaces concrete items, or when the question targets a single named activity.

payload.name: Include plan memories when searching planned events
payload.description: When a question asks about a planned or upcoming event/activity (e.g., 'planning', 'plans to', 'next summer'), search memory with memory_kinds including both 'event' and 'plan' instead of only 'event'.
content: Before answering a question about what someone plans to do or an upcoming event, include both 'event' and 'plan' as memory_kinds in the first search.

If the initial hybrid search with event+plan returns no relevant plan memory, run one follow-up structured search with memory_kinds=['plan'] and keywords from the question before concluding the answer is not in memory.

candidates.solves: Search failures occur when a question about future plans is answered while the agent restricts retrieval to memory_kind 'event', which excludes stored plan memories that directly state the planned activity. Future questions phrased with 'planning', 'plans to', or 'upcoming' should retrieve both 'event' and 'plan' kinds. Do not apply this when the question concerns only completed past events or current states, where 'event' kind is sufficient.

payload.name: Morphological-Expansion-For-Event-Counts
payload.description: When a question asks to count or enumerate all memories of an action or event, expand the action verb to its morphological variants and synonyms (e.g., win/won/wins/winning) and continue searching until a search returns no new relevant memories.
content: If the question asks for a count or full enumeration of events involving an action verb (e.g., 'how many games has John mentioned winning'), do not rely only on the exact keyword form. Search with morphological variants and synonyms of the verb (win, won, winning, wins, beat, victory) using keyword and semantic/hybrid strategies.

Before answering, verify recall: run one more expanded search if the latest search returned previously unseen memories that match the action; stop when a search returns no new relevant memories, then compute the count from all uniquely retrieved matching memories.

candidates.solves: The general failure is that exact-keyword search misses morphological variants of the action verb, causing undercounting when a question requires enumerating all matching event memories. This Skill applies when a future question asks how many or enumerate all instances of an action/event, where all relevant memories must be collected. It must not apply to single-fact lookup questions that are answered by one explicit match, where variant expansion is unnecessary.

payload.name: Count-Event Synonym Retrieval
payload.description: When a user asks a count or frequency question about a person's experiences (e.g., 'how many times has X been rejected?') and the first keyword search returns no direct evidence, use this to search with the event noun and synonyms before answering 'no information'.
content: If the question asks for a count of a repeated experience (how many times, how often, number of), search using the noun form of the event (e.g., 'rejection' for 'rejected') and synonyms for the object (e.g., 'screenplay', 'script', 'creative work') in addition to the literal wording.

If the first search returns no direct evidence, run at least one more retrieval with an expanded synonym query or a different strategy (e.g., hybrid or semantic) before concluding information is unavailable.
Stop expanding once the relevant event memories are found, usually after 2-3 distinct queries; do not exhaustively search for every possible synonym.

candidates.solves: This addresses retrieval failure when a count/frequency question is answered with 'no information' because the only keyword search used exact question phrasing and missed memories stored with morphological or synonymous terms (e.g., 'rejection' vs 'rejected', 'screenplay' vs 'scripts'). It applies to future questions asking how many times a person experienced an event where the first search returns no direct evidence. It must not apply to non-count questions or when the first search already retrieves relevant memories.

payload.name: Decompose composite questions into sub-searches
payload.description: When a question asks for an activity or item that must satisfy two independent conditions about the same person—such as something they would enjoy doing AND that benefits their pet—decompose retrieval into separate sub-searches before combining evidence.
content: Before searching, split the question into its independent conditions (for example, 'activity Andrew enjoys' and 'activity involving his dog'). Do not rely on a single composite query.

Run at least one targeted search for each condition separately (e.g., hobbies/preferences/interests; pet-related memories), then intersect the returned memory sets to identify candidates satisfying both conditions.
Stop once each condition has at least one supporting memory; do not add further expansion searches.

candidates.solves: Single composite queries for multi-condition questions (e.g., an activity a person enjoys that also involves their pet) over-weight one condition and miss memories supporting each condition separately. Applies when a question requires combining a person's enjoyment/hobby with a pet-related benefit. Does not apply when one memory already directly answers the question.

payload.name: Enumeration-of-Acquired-Items Retrieval
payload.description: When a user asks what items someone bought, made, or acquired for a specific person, pet, or household (e.g., 'what items has Audrey bought or made for her dogs?'), use category-expanded searches before concluding the list is complete.
content: Before the first search on an enumeration question, add concrete category nouns for the recipient type (e.g., for pets: toys, beds, collars, tags, leashes, food, treats, bowls) plus synonyms of the action (bought/purchased/ordered/acquired, made/created/crafted/built) to both the query and keywords.

After the initial results, do not generate follow-up keywords solely from items already seen; instead, probe each remaining category from your expanded list that has not yet appeared with a keyword or structured search until it is covered or the memory pool is exhausted.
Stop when every candidate category has been probed or an additional category search returns no new relevant memories and the evidence already supports answering all parts of the question.

candidates.solves: When a user asks for the complete set of items someone bought or made for a recipient (person, pet, household), the search may miss relevant memories because keywords echo only the first results and synonyms (e.g., 'purchased') or item categories (e.g., 'beds') are never probed. This Skill applies to such enumeration questions where completeness is expected. It must not be used for a single-fact confirmation (e.g., 'Did X buy a bed?') or when the user explicitly limits the question to one category.

payload.name: Enumerate acquisition events for count questions
payload.description: When a question asks how many pets or other owned possessions a person has as of a specific date, and the answer requires counting acquisition events (adoptions, purchases) rather than an explicit stored count.
content: Before answering a count question (e.g., 'how many pets does X have as of <date>?'), search for acquisition events for that person before the date using queries like 'adopted', 'adopted a dog/puppy/pup', 'got a pet', 'bought', or 'welcomed', plus the person's name; set structured entity to the person, memory_kind to 'event', and target_time to the date.

Enumerate all distinct named pets/items from those event memories with world_start before the target time; count each distinct name once. Do not stop after one existing pet or after a plan to get another; continue until no further acquisition events are found.

Do not rely on numeric phrasing ('how many', 'count', 'number of pets') as the only retrieval query, because memories rarely store such counts; use count searches only as a supplement after the acquisition-event search.

candidates.solves: General failure: count questions are answered using only direct numeric phrasing like "how many" or "count", which misses the underlying acquisition events (adoptions, purchases) that determine the total. Applies when a future question asks for the number of a person's pets or similar possessions as of a specific date and the memory store contains multiple acquisition events rather than an explicit count. Do not apply when the store already has an explicit count memory or when the question asks for identity or attributes of a known pet rather than a count.

payload.name: Count owned pets via acquisition events
payload.description: When a question asks how many of a pet/animal type a person has or owns, use acquisition/ownership event searches before concluding no information.
content: When the question is a count of owned items (e.g., 'how many dogs does Andrew have?'), run an acquisition-focused search using the person's name plus ownership terms such as 'adopted', 'adoption', 'owns', 'got', and pet-type synonyms (dog/puppy/pup, cat/kitten).
Aggregate distinct named individuals from current (active) event memories about that person; exclude plans, considerations, other people's pets, and repeated mentions of the same pet.
Stop after one focused acquisition search if all owned items are identified or it returns no new candidates; do not exhaustively expand.

candidates.solves: The failure mechanism is that count-of-owned-things questions are answered after a single generic keyword query that misses the adoption/ownership event memories naming each item, so the agent falsely reports no information. This Skill applies when a future question asks 'how many X does Y have/own' where X is a pet or possession, and the needed evidence is distributed across acquisition events. operations.name: Preference-Based Suggestion Retrieval
operations.description: Use when a question asks what a person recommends, suggests, likes, or considers a favorite, and explicit recommendation/preference memories may be missing.
content: When the question asks for a person's recommendation, suggestion, or favorite, do not restrict retrieval to the literal word 'recommend' or 'suggested'; also run a preference-oriented search combining the person with terms like enjoys, likes, favorite, plays, or relevant hobby keywords.

Prioritize explicit preference or favorite memories over incidental activity mentions; if initial retrieval lacks them, run structured searches filtered to the person with memory_kind 'preference' or predicates like favorite/enjoy.

Accept a candidate memory only if it directly links the named entity to that person through stated preference or hobby matching the question context; stop after one preference pass or when preference memories cover the items you will claim.

operations.name: Alternative Activity Retrieval
operations.description: Use when a question asks for an alternative to a stated activity or domain (e.g., 'instead of', 'after', 'outside', 'if not'), and the first search returns only the named activity.
content: If the question asks for an alternative or replacement for a known activity/domain, run a second search that does not include the replaced activity as a keyword; use the person's name with terms like 'plan', 'prefer', 'decide', 'hobby', 'interest', 'enjoys', or 'want'.
Include profile/interest memories in the search, because alternatives are often recorded as stated plans or preferences rather than event memories.
Stop as soon as you find a memory describing a planned or preferred activity different from the one in the question; do not search for exhaustive alternatives.

Run additional targeted searches for uncovered common categories (e.g., outdoor, winter sports, reading, creative, fitness) and for activities besides a named primary activity, using structured event/activity searches.
Stop when two consecutive targeted searches return no new distinct activity categories; answer from the union of all retrieved memories.
